title: How to Gamify Chores: Cleaning Playlists, Dice and Other Tricks That Make It Fun
description: Boring chores are hard for busy brains to start. Gamify cleaning with playlists, chore dice, races and rewards. 9 easy ideas for you and the kids.
intro:
Our brains are not built for boring. A task with no deadline, no novelty and no reward (hello, folding towels) can feel almost impossible to start, even when we really want it done.

But put a timer on it, add a song, turn it into a race? Suddenly we're moving. That's not a trick of willpower. Interest and urgency are what get a lot of us going, so it makes sense to add a little of both to chores.

Here are nine ways to gamify cleaning, from a playlist that works as a timer to a deck of chore cards. Pick one that sounds fun today and try it for 15 minutes.

sections.heading: 1. Make a cleaning playlist that doubles as a timer
sections.body:
Build a playlist that's exactly 15 or 20 minutes long. When it starts, you clean. When it ends, you're done, no matter where you are.

Put your most upbeat songs first to get you off the couch, and a favorite at the end so the finish line feels good. Use the same playlist every time. After a few weeks, the first song alone can get you moving.

sections.heading: 2. Beat the song
sections.body: Pick one song and one job. Can you unload the dishwasher before the chorus? Clear the counter before the song ends? Short races make small chores feel like a challenge instead of a chore.

sections.heading: 3. Roll the chore dice
sections.body:
Write six quick chores on a list and number them 1 to 6. Roll a die and do whatever comes up. Roll again if you have energy.

Random choice takes away the "where do I start?" freeze. The die decides, you follow. Kids love this one, too.

sections.heading: 4. Pull a chore card
sections.body:
Write small chores on index cards: wipe the bathroom sink, gather all the cups, fold one basket. Keep them in a jar. Pull one or two a day.

Make some cards fun: "dance for one song," "pick your snack." A bit of surprise keeps it interesting.

sections.heading: 5. Play 'Ten Things'
sections.body: Walk into any room and put away ten things. Count out loud. That's it. It works because ten is a clear finish line, and once you've hit ten, you often keep going without trying.

sections.heading: 6. Use a points board
sections.body:
Make a simple chart on the fridge. Every chore earns points: 1 for small jobs, 3 for big ones. Hit a goal number and get a reward you pick ahead of time: a fancy coffee, a new book, a movie night.

For families, a shared goal works great. "When the family hits 100 points, we get pizza night."

sections.heading: 7. Race the kids (or race yourself)
sections.body: Set a timer for five minutes and see who can pick up the most toys, socks or cups. Or race your own time: how fast can you clean the bathroom sink? Write the time down and try to beat it next week.

sections.heading: 8. Clean with a body double
sections.body: Call a friend and clean at the same time, or put on a "clean with me" video. Having someone else working beside you, even on a screen, can make it easier to start and keep going.

sections.heading: 9. Pair it with something you love
sections.body: Save a favorite podcast, audiobook or show for cleaning time only. Now cleaning is the only time you get the next episode. It's a reward built right into the task.

sections.heading: When the game stops working
sections.body: New games get old. That's normal for our brains, not a failure. When a trick stops working, switch to another one on this list. Rotating between three or four keeps things fresh.

outro:
Cleaning doesn't have to be fun to get done. But a little fun makes it a whole lot easier to start, and starting is the hardest part.
